searchText: <@543900561460822016> <@425279588009246720> 1559 doesn't preclude legacy transactions from being included, they just don't get the UX benefit of gas estimations or payingmindmum required gas price. I have a PR out against 1559 that makes this change to the spec, so legacy transactions never go away. In that case, what do you think about having a third tx type in 2718 with the same functionality as the legacy tx that follows the new hashing / signing rules? <@!543900561460822016> The tentative plan is to remove all of the new transaction types from 2718 and create a *separate* EIP that defines two new transaction types that are just thin wrappers around legacy transactions. Since we aren't immediately deprecating legacy transactions with 2718, we no longer need the new transaction types to be paired with the new wrapper type. Most likely the two would go out in a hard fork together, but it isn't a hard requirement. So, over the wire are legacy txs still allowed (with legacy encoding)? Yes. Will the new ones follow the new “standard” hashing and signing schemes? The two new ones that I will be proposing will be signature compatible with legacy transactions, but otherwise will follow all of the new rules. What is the advantage of having them signature compatible of legacy txs will continue to be valid? <@!543900561460822016> so someone with a signature from a long time ago can still do a transfer. Or someone with a hardware wallet that cannot be upgraded can still execute transactions. We don't want people to end up in a situation where their funds are inaccessible because they are only able to sign legacy transactions. But I thought you said above that legacy txs will continue to be valid? In that case, why can’t hardware wallets continue signing and propagating legacy transactions? We would like to eventually like to get rid of legacy transaction wire/block format, but we'll probably *always* retain the legacy transaction signature validity. The two new transaction types I'll propose in a separate EIP will maintain signature compatibility with legacy transactions, but have the new format on the wire and in blocks. <@!543900561460822016> In that case, why continue allowing legacy txs over the wire in the first place? 1. If we *can* split up the EIP we *should* split up the EIP. 2. Transaction propagation is a separate problem from block generation/validation and we cannot change both at once. 3. Transaction hashes will change with the new transaction type, and creates some complexity around the transition. 4. Receipts change, and while we can downgrade the receipt it would be cleaner to introduce new JSON-RPC endpoints for new transaction receipts, and if we do that it takes time for applications to migrate to the new endpoint. Summary: There is a lot of complexity around deprecation, it is easier to handle it separate from the new type EIPs. <@!211091239112671234> turbogeth isn't planning on syncing with yolov2 at this time. Ok. I don't have a strong opinion on whether to include the previous eips or not, but I'd lean slightly towards including them, so we can continue fuzzing it The reason we are not planning YoloV2 at the moment because I would like to avoid over-committing (trying to do more work that we can realistically accomplish), which I encouraged other people to avoid, but it is obviously up to them to decide what to do

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: We would like to eventually like to get rid of legacy transaction wire/block format, but we'll probably *always* retain the legacy transaction signature validity.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: The two new transaction types I'll propose in a separate EIP will maintain signature compatibility with legacy transactions, but have the new format on the wire and in blocks.

excerpts.author: lightclient
excerpts.content: In that case, why continue allowing legacy txs over the wire in the first place?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
1. If we *can* split up the EIP we *should* split up the EIP.
2. Transaction propagation is a separate problem from block generation/validation and we cannot change both at once.
3. Transaction hashes will change with the new transaction type, and creates some complexity around the transition.
4. Receipts change, and while we can downgrade the receipt it would be cleaner to introduce new JSON-RPC endpoints for new transaction receipts, and if we do that it takes time for applications to migrate to the new endpoint.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Summary: There is a lot of complexity around deprecation, it is easier to handle it separate from the new type EIPs.
